node.label: Mary Ritter Beard
node.description: Argues that women helped make historical institutions and events, and that histories must investigate their activity rather than assume universal passivity. Her work combines historical argument, collaborative synthesis and efforts to preserve and teach women’s records.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Woman as Force in History: A Study in Traditions and Realities (1946); work supporting women’s documentary collections, including the Sophia Smith Collection. Her account of agency remains open to criticism about differences among women and structures of power.
node.scope_note: Woman as Force in History (1946) challenges the subject-sex tradition through legal and other historical inquiry; its preface does not establish that agency cancels subordination. WCWA (1935–1940) and Smith collecting depended on Schwimmer, Grierson, donors and other collaborators. Voss-Hubbard documents Black women’s limited authority and funding within WCWA. Cott’s 1991 editorial recovery uses letters preserved by correspondents. Mary’s distinct work coexists with collaboration with Charles; legal cases and specific later theoretical criticism remain to be checked.

incident_edges.relationship: argues for women’s historical agency and supports documentary recovery
incident_edges.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. The complete 1946 preface supplies the attributed agency argument; Voss-Hubbard reconstructs collaborative archival practice and its institutional/racial limits. Neither proves universal emancipation or sole founding.
incident_edges.map_label: Agency, records and contested archival practice

incident_edges.relationship: invites comparison between earlier agency-centered history and later recovery groupings
incident_edges.evidence_note: An editorial test of Hunt’s grouping, not a claim that Beard adopted the later language of identity politics. Beard questions the historical subject-sex premise and equality as a sufficient guide in her preface. This remains a comparison with later identity questions, not their origin or a shared unified position.
incident_edges.map_label: Historical agency and the category of women

incident_edges.relationship: Schwimmer and Grierson help shape archival projects through proposal, disagreement and sustained institutional work
incident_edges.evidence_note: Voss-Hubbard pp. 19–30 differentiates Schwimmer’s pacifist project from the broader WCWA and Grierson’s collecting/access work at Smith. Collective practice is not doctrinal agreement or sole authorship.

incident_edges.relationship: Black women’s archival participation exposes unequal authority and support within WCWA
incident_edges.evidence_note: Voss-Hubbard pp. 20–21 reports Thurman/Bethune/NCNW involvement and dissatisfaction, with no Black directors and limited support for fieldwork. This criticism of organizational practice is mediated through the 1995 study, not a claim that all Black women shared one response or a direct refutation of the 1946 book.
incident_edges.map_label: WCWA: racial inclusion, authority and resources

incident_edges.relationship: Mary Beard coauthors broad histories of American civilization with Charles Beard
incident_edges.evidence_note: The Rise of American Civilization (1927) and America in Midpassage (1939) are documented collaborative works. Precise division of authorship and identical interpretations are not established; her separate women’s-history work remains distinct.

incident_edges.relationship: Charles Beard participates in the documented partnership of historical writing
incident_edges.evidence_note: The reciprocal contribution names a particular coauthor rather than a uniform school acting on Mary Beard. No surviving correspondence between the couple is claimed, nor a precise allocation of chapters.

incident_edges.relationship: Recovers Beard’s historical work through a selected edition of her letters, editorial commentary and an introductory assessment.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Cott’s own1991 preface explains selection, commentary and documentary treatment, including omitted late letters attacking Charles Beard’s critics and the role of the literary heirs. Her introduction treats Mary as a historian in her own right. This is scholarly editorial recovery, not evidence that Mary formally mentored Cott. The full correspondence remains unread.

incident_edges.relationship: Questions Beard’s treatment of the conflict between domestic responsibilities and women’s opportunities in public life.
incident_edges.evidence_note: In the selected1991 introduction paragraph beginning She considered, Cott appreciates Beard’s radical challenge to private/public divisions but observes that she looked away from conflicting domestic and public demands. Cott finds her civilizing-power account more comfortable and persuasive for societies with less elaborated public/private divisions. This particular reservation accompanies substantive recovery and praise; it does not reject Beard’s whole work. The source jumps from the displayed48 archive passage to this domesticity paragraph without a connecting page header; its original printed page is uncertain. The next sentence is cut off and supplies no claim.

named_group_routes.relationship: Davis’s comparative biographies develop through women’s-history teaching, source discovery and revised questions of significance
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Davis names the 1971 course with Conway and Colie’s Glikl suggestion in her acknowledgments. Her prologue and conclusion compare three lives while retaining religious difference and colonial power. This primary selection supplements the existing catalogue description; it is not a full source audit or a claim that women’s history originated biography.
named_group_routes.map_label: Davis, Conway and Colie: teaching into research

named_group_routes.relationship: Beard connects political institutions to economic interests
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Applies to the Progressive side of this paired node, not to all consensus history; economic interpretation does not by itself establish Marxist affiliation. Preface and chapter XI opening supply Beard’s own framing; his constitutional data and inferred motives have not been replicated.

named_group_routes.relationship: invites comparison of materialist explanation with Beard’s economic interpretation
named_group_routes.evidence_note: No Marxist identity or simple derivation is attributed to Beard, and no common economic method to consensus historians.

named_group_routes.relationship: intersects in Becker’s and Beard’s arguments about interpretation and objectivity
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of the cited approaches, not a claim of transmission or agreement.

named_group_routes.relationship: Benson explicitly challenges the economic-determinist interpretation he attributes to Turner and Beard
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Chapter VIII opening names both historians. The target is the Progressive side of the paired entry and a specified interpretation; it is not criticism of every argument by them or every consensus historian.
named_group_routes.map_label: Benson: criticism of economic-determinist voting history

named_group_routes.relationship: Beard cites Cunningham on testing historical hypotheses
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Chapter 1 invokes William Cunningham’s methodological advice. This specific citation does not establish agreement on all economic interpretations.

named_group_routes.relationship: Libby’s sectional mapping supplies Beard with a resource
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Beard’s preface and chapter 1 explicitly credit Libby; the latter’s introduction explains the procedure and its proxies.
Chapter 1 criticizes a named national-history account while recognizing documentary scholarship. Beard’s characterization is a polemic, not an exhaustive description of Bancroft.

named_group_routes.relationship: Hartz disputes Marx’s explanation of socialist ideology
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Chapter 1 section 2 proposes an alternative relation between feudal heritage and socialist thought. This is Hartz’s claim alone; the existing Beard/materialism comparison remains distinct.

named_group_routes.relationship: Bederman cites Lears’s account of neurasthenia among the resources for explaining anxieties about allegedly depleted white middle-class male vitality.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Body14/n54 uses No Place of Grace (1981),49–57 with Gosling, the jointly authored Haller study, Rotundo and Lutz, alongside contemporary George Beard. This is a specific plural resource, not an exclusive origin for the book’s argument or an endorsement of the historical disease categories. The Lears original remains unread.

records.context: Argues for women’s historical agency while promoting records, catalogues and teaching; her general category of women and institutional practice require critical assessment.

records.context: Earlier women’s historical agency tests the limits of the later umbrella.

Addendum 2026-10-26: Fresh selected authorial preface xi and discontinuous introduction passages including displayed48 and later unpaginated text recovered through indexed primary transcription at https://dokumen.pub/a-woman-making-history-mary-ritter-beard-through-her-letters-9780300162585.html. Own editorial account explains selection, interspersed commentary, omitted late letters attacking husband’s critics, ellipses, supplied brackets and corrections. An unpaginated retained paragraph beginning She considered identifies a particular limitation in Beard’s treatment of domesticity and public opportunity. Full letters and complete introduction remain unread; no all141-letters reading claim. Earlier publisher-metadata-only verification remains a historical record, extended rather than overwritten.

verification.note: Public OCR read: title/edition; complete prologue pp. 1–4, conclusion pp. 203–216 and acknowledgments pp. 340–344; selected Glikl opening pp. 6–8 and conclusion notes 1–8/start of 9. Main chapters and remaining notes not fully read. Prologue is an imagined October 1994 dialogue. Certeau and Foucault are explicit resources; editions/translations and collaboration are discussed. Addendum 2026-10-18: Revision 1.144: the stored PDF URL now returns HTML; the review was read via WebFetch extraction at https://reviews.history.ac.uk/review/1732/print. Julia McClure, review of Lynn Hunt, Writing History in the Global Era (Norton, 2014), Reviews in History no. 1732 (19 February 2015). Her summary: globalization has become a dominant "paradigm" filling the place of Marxism, modernization, the Annales school and identity politics, privileging economics and macro trends and threatening to overshadow "society" and "self"; Hunt surveys the cultural theories (Foucault, Derrida) she helped bring into history, defending their gains and acknowledging their limits; Hunt is quoted as saying globalization "potentially threatens to wash away the gains of the last decades of cultural history" (p. 59, as McClure cites it). McClure's criticisms: no proponents of the paradigm named; global history equated with the history of globalization; Hunt's own standpoint on universal values needs the scrutiny she applies to Mignolo. The book itself is unread. The second research pass (evidence-hunt.pass2.md §6) read the review in full (4-page PDF) and records Hunt's words with the book's pages as McClure gives them: globalization "asserts the inescapability of the process, the primacy of economics in driving it" (p. 55); "the globalization paradigm reinstates the very suppositions that cultural theories had criticized, and thus potentially threatens to wash away the gains of the last decades of cultural history" (p. 59); "historians need to contest the terrain it now claims, using the tools held out by cultural theories while remaining mindful of their limitations" (p. 43); "is it a Trojan horse that threatens to bring back old paradigms rather than offering a truly new one?" (p. 52). McClure: "Hunt's criticism of the globalization paradigm is not a criticism of historical genre, but of ideology."
